newsitem.title: USA: Solid growth ahead for U.S. economy-Conference Bd.
newsitem.headline: Solid growth ahead for U.S. economy-Conference Bd.

text.p: The Conference Board on Monday said strength in the U.S. economy will continue throughout 1997 and into 1998, fueled by a buoyant consumer sector and continued growth in construction and business investment.
"The economic strength evident in the first quarter is no fluke," said Gail Fosler, senior vice president and chief economist of The Conference Board.
"The domestic U.S. economy will outpace expectations for most of this year, (and) the second half of 1997 may be somewhat stronger than the first half," she said.
Consumers will gain confidence to spend in an environment with low interest rates and higher wages, she said. The Conference Board forecast consumer spending growth to top 3.0 percent in 1997.
"Even though interest rates have moved up a notch, these relatively modest increases are swamped by strong consumer fundamentals," said Fosler.
An interest rate hike in May is probable, but the pace of interest rate increases is likely to slow after that, The Conference Board said.
Treasury bond yields will exhibit some of the same volatility evident in short-term interest rates, it said.
The Conference Board projected the 30-year Treasury bond's yield would hit 7.5 percent to 7.75 percent by yearend.
"Higher bond yields are likely to come in 'waves' rather than a rush, as in 1994," said Fosler. "This makes the current period a particularly treacherous environment from a financial perspective."
But Fosler said growth in the domestic economy will be tempered by a swelling trade deficit.
Imports growth should accelerate and exports growth should decelerate by yearend as a strong dollar continues to pressure the U.S. international trade balance, The Conference Board said.

Looking at wages, whether measured by average hourly earnings or the core wage component of the Employment Cost Index (ECI), The Conference Board asserted they are "moving unmistakably upward, with both measures probably approaching 4.5 percent by the end of 1997."
"The steady upward pressure on wages will be reflected in industrial prices ... (which) are now rising rapidly, supported in part by rising capacity utilization rates," it said.
